title: F6 – Business strategy: business models and generic strategies
source: Zusammenfassung von Session 5 „Business Strategy (Part 1/2)“ mit dem Fall „AI Wars“ und Ryall (2013)

blocks.text: Business strategy: how to compete in a market. Corporate strategy: where to compete. Business strategy is a choice about how the organization performs the primary and support activities of the value chain to create value – for single businesses or strategic business units (SBUs).
A business model is an arrangement of activities describing a value proposition and how it is achieved: value creation, value configuration, value capture.

Two dimensions of competitive positioning: cost vs value (differentiation) and broad vs narrow scope → four generic strategies. The risk is being “stuck in the middle” – unless activities are compartmentalized or the offer is innovative enough (blue ocean).
Value creation: what is offered to which customer segment – which needs, which solution?
Value configuration: how the elements of the value chain are organized to deliver the value proposition.
Value capture: why does the model generate a margin – where are the sources of revenues and costs?
Airbnb: value for guests (finding housing) and hosts (renting it out); configured as a multi-sided platform; captured by Airbnb through booking commissions and by hosts through guests' payments.

Value creation ≠ value capture (Ryall 2013): a firm can create a lot of value and keep little of it. Who captures the surplus depends on who has credible alternatives in the value network (Amazon's early book sales: easy switching → low markups; Apple iPod + iTunes: ecosystem and loyalty → strong capture).
Cost advantage: structurally lower costs than competitors → lower prices with higher market share, or higher margins.
Value advantage through differentiation: a unique source of value → higher willingness-to-pay (WTP) → higher prices or market share.
Created value = generated value for the demand (WTP) − costs. A competitor can have a cost advantage, a value advantage, or – rarely – both (dual advantage).
1. Cost leadership (low cost, broad market): systematically lower costs, often in inbound and outbound logistics; standardization (McDonald's in “The Founder”). Three sources of lower costs:
children: Costs of input resources: raw materials, labour
Economies of scale: average cost falls with output – up to diseconomies of scale (U-shaped long-run average cost)
Economies of learning (experience curve): unit cost falls with cumulated experience – capital and labour productivity

blocks.text: Structure for cost leadership: functional, simple reporting lines, few layers, centralized staff focusing on process improvement and cost reduction, specialized jobs, operations as the main function. Challenges: sustaining low costs (labour regulation, rare inputs), keeping acceptable quality, preserving human rights – labour is not a resource like capital.

2. Differentiation (high differentiation, broad market): uniqueness on a dimension valued by customers, often through innovation (Apple, Netflix) → higher WTP. Sources: material attributes (unique technology) and non-material attributes (service, reputation, brand). Structure: complex, flexible reporting, marketing and product R&D as main functions, less specialized jobs. Challenges: costly and risky innovation, costs still matter, rivals may deliver the same value at lower cost, WTP is not unlimited, risk of being too different.
3. Focused cost leadership (low cost, narrow market): a specific geography (local restaurant), customer type or activity (commodity fruit market).
4. Focused differentiation (high differentiation, narrow market), often high-end: Ladurée macarons, rare-disease medicine, professional extreme sports.

Juicero (USD 120m VC, juicing press at USD 700 then 400): perceived value is not enough – the price must be justified by substantial added value. A disassembled press showed an over-engineered machine; bags could be squeezed by hand.
Organizations are stuck in the middle when their positioning between cost leadership and differentiation is unclear AND this leads to bad performance.
JCPenney (near bankruptcy 2020): cut prices but could not match Walmart on cost; added brand shops but could not match Macy's on value.
Exceptions: compartmentalized activities, or a blue ocean that combines lower costs and differentiation – an advantage usually limited in time.

Google invented the Transformer (2017) but OpenAI commercialized it; by 2025 Gemini is technically competitive – the constraint is Google's business model: generative answers substitute for ad-funded search (cannibalization).

Five Forces: suppliers powerful (Nvidia 70–95 % of AI chips; superstar AI talent, no non-competes in California); buyers powerful (free or cheap services, low switching costs); entry barriers lowered by open weights, public data and known architectures.

Business model: unlike classic software, every query has a real marginal cost, and usage is skewed and unbounded. Responses: caps, tiers (free / USD 20 / USD 200), routing to cheaper models; and advertising, because most users never pay (Google earns ~1.6 cents per search from 6.25bn users).

Three ways to play a gold rush: dig for gold (build and sell the best model – structurally costly), sell shovels (chips, cloud – profit whoever wins), make jewellery (own the complements – Meta, Chrome, Android, Workspace – and want the gold cheap). Google tries all three at once.
An arrangement of activities that describes a value proposition and the ways of achieving it (creation, configuration, capture).
The maximum price a customer is ready to pay; raised by differentiation.
Unit costs fall as output increases (until diseconomies of scale set in).
Unit costs fall with cumulated production experience (learning curve).
Unclear position between cost leadership and differentiation, resulting in poor performance.

sections.heading: Further thinking: using F6 in the exam

blocks.text: Classify the firm on both axes (cost vs differentiation, broad vs narrow) with evidence, then check consistency of its value chain and structure with that choice.

For “how to improve profitability” questions, separate value creation from value capture: raise WTP, cut costs, or capture a larger share (pricing, fees, bargaining power) – and name the trade-off for the position and identity.
